在烏干達布干達的木琴傳統中，阿卡丁達與amadinda同屬此類樂器。來源記載am: In the xylophone tradition of Buganda in Uganda, the akadinda and the amadinda belong to the same class of instrument. The source records that the amadinda is played mainly by three people, two players sitting face to face on either side of the same set of keys and playing together in a fast interlocking technique. In listening, notice that it has no gourd resonators and none of the buzzing that other African xylophones usually have, which is how you can tell it from African xylophones with gourd resonators or a buzzing timbre.
木琴起源不明，有學者認為源於東南亞，約公元500年傳入非洲，另有學者主張非洲獨立: The origin of the xylophone is unknown: some scholars think it came from Southeast Asia and reached Africa around AD 500, while others argue for an independent African origin. The akadinda and amadinda come from Buganda in what is now Uganda. The amadinda is made of twelve logs tuned to a pentatonic scale and is played mainly by three people; two sit facing each other and strike the same keys in a fast interlocking technique. It has no gourd resonators and does not produce the buzzing timbre common to other African xylophones.
演奏時以琴槌敲擊木鍵發聲。與阿卡丁達同類的amadinda主要由三人演奏，兩名演: It is played by striking wooden keys with beaters. The amadinda, which belongs with the akadinda, is played mainly by three people, two sitting opposite each other and striking the same set of wooden keys in a fast interlocking rhythm. A beginner can first practise a steady stroke on the keys, then come in interlocking with another player. Instruments of this kind have no gourd resonators and produce no buzzing timbre.

Compared with many African xylophones, the amadinda, also from Buganda, is made of twelve logs tuned to a pentatonic scale and has no gourd resonators and no buzzing timbre. Xylophones can generally use beaters of different hardness for a softer or lighter timbre, but the source does not say whether the akadinda does.
